summary: This note is an encyclopedia-style overview of walking (ambulation) as a gait of terrestrial locomotion. It covers how walking differs from running, health benefits, evolutionary origins including hominin bipedalism, biomechanics, variants such as Nordic walking and racewalking, recreation and tourism, walkability, robotics, mathematical models, and walking in animals like horses, elephants and insects.
one_line: Comprehensive overview of walking as a gait, covering its mechanics, evolution, health benefits, variants, recreational and urban aspects, robotics and animal walking.
key_facts: Walking is defined by an "inverted pendulum" gait in which the body vaults over the stiff limb or limbs with each step, and applies regardless of limb number, even to arthropods.
The average human walking speed at crosswalks is about 5.0 km/h (1.4 m/s, 3.1 mph); a brisk walking speed is around 6.5 km/h, and champion racewalkers average more than 14 km/h over 20 km.
An average human child achieves independent walking at around 11 months old.
A 2023 study in the European Journal of Preventive Cardiology found 2,337 steps a day reduced risk of cardiovascular death and 3,967 steps a day reduced risk of death from any cause.
CDC data cited say people with diabetes who walked two or more hours a week lowered all-cause mortality by 39 percent.
Footprints discovered on a former shore in Kenya suggest ancestors of modern humans walked in ways very similar to today as long as 3 million years ago.
A 2007 study found human locomotion costs about seventy-five percent less energy than chimpanzee locomotion, and chimpanzee bipedalism costs roughly ten percent more than quadrupedal walking.
Human walking uses a double pendulum strategy and can save approximately sixty-five percent of the energy used by exploiting gravity.
Nordic walking with poles has been estimated to produce up to a 46% increase in energy consumption compared with walking without poles.

The International Four Days Marches Nijmegen in the Netherlands, held annually since 1909 and based at Nijmegen since 1916, is the world's largest multi-day walking event, with over 40,000 participants.
The Labor Day walk on Mackinac Bridge, Michigan draws over 60,000 participants and is the largest single-day walking event.
The Lijnbaan in Rotterdam, opened in 1953, was the first purpose-built pedestrian street in Europe; Copenhagen's centre became a pedestrian zone in 1962.
In 2009, Japanese roboticist Tomotaka Takahashi developed Ropid, a robot capable of getting up, walking, running and jumping.
A horse's walk is a four-beat gait averaging about 4 mph (6.4 km/h), while elephants walk and use a faster running-like gait with top speed of 18 km/h.
